extracted.intended_audience: aspiring orators, students of rhetoric, and writers of speeches
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for composing and judging persuasive public speeches in the classical (Roman/Greek) tradition, emphasizing elocution, structure, delivery, and rhetorical devices, with examples and warnings from historical practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion as the chief business
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That which the Greeks call [Peitho] (i.e. Persuasion) ... it is the chief business of an Orator to effect' (Ennius calls an orator the 'quintessence of Persuasion').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary aim of oratory is to persuade (suada/peitho). The text treats the orator as the embodiment of Persuasion and praises speakers who can make ideas compelling to an audience (example: Cethegus praised for being the 'very marrow and quintessence of Persuasion').

rubrics_metrics.name: Neatness and clarity in stating the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the two principal qualities required in an Orator, are to be neat and clear in stating the nature of his subject'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An orator must present the subject plainly and clearly so the audience understands the issue. This is cited as a foundational requirement paired with the capacity to move the passions; clarity is contrasted with mere ornamentation or excessive antiquated phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warmth and force in moving the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'warm and forcible in moving the passions'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional power matters: 'he who fires and inflames his audience, will always effect more than he who can barely inform and amuse them.' Pathos (moving the passions) is a practical, outcome-focused quality — it often outweighs mere exposition. Examples: Galba praised for pathetic force that swayed juries and saved clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness / mellifluence of elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: Ennius's praise: M. Cornelius Cethegus 'so much admired for his mellifluent tongue' ('suaviloquenti').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sweet, pleasant delivery ('mellifluent' elocution) is a principal ornament of eloquence; it makes speech agreeable and memorable. The text contrasts this with 'insufferably harsh' modern speakers who 'bark' rather than speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Cato and Lysias are commended for 'acuteness, their elegance, their agreeable humour, and their brevity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness is praised as a virtue (attic neatness). Excessive pomp or verbosity can obscure sense; brevity can be powerful though it must be balanced with clarity and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength, vigor, and forceful diction
rubrics_metrics.description: References to 'strength of arm' and 'strenuous and forcible' manner of speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond sweetness and neatness, oratory needs vigor — forceful, energetic diction and reasoning. The Greeks and Romans balanced graceful style with substantial force; speakers who combined both were most effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and polished style (measured flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for 'easy gracefulness of the Greeks' and speakers 'distinguished by the measured flow of his language, and a style regularly polished and improved by art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A polished, gracefully flowing style (cadence, smooth sentences) is an ideal — cultivated by study and imitation of good models (Greek examples). This stylistic polish should not sacrifice substance or vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of tropes and figures of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the chief beauty of composition results from the frequent use of those ... which they call Tropes, and ... Figures'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical devices (figures, tropes) and varied linguistic 'attitudes' are crucial ornaments that supply variety and elegance. The text notes Cato's abundant use of figures and recommends learning and applying such devices judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cadence, number, and sentence rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: 'add the improvements of number and cadence, give an easier turn to his sentences, and regulate the structure and connection of his words'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal elements like rhythm, periodic sentence structure, and cadence (the musicality of phrasing) materially affect persuasiveness. Improving 'number and cadence' can modernize and clarify older, harsher styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt language to the present (modernize archaic expressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His language indeed has an antiquated air... only change and modernize it'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors with ancient or archaic diction should be revised for contemporary intelligibility and grace: update phrases, smooth structure, and adjust expression while retaining substance. Anti-pattern: slavishly preserving obsolete expressions that hinder comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between natural passion and polished writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 'spoke much better than they were able to write' — passion fuels spoken eloquence but may not transfer to prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the difference between speech-in-performance and written text. Frequent writing and revision improve translatability from oration to text; but genuine fervor in delivery cannot always be replicated on the page. Don't expect every great speaker to be an equally great writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation, industriousness, and frequent writing
rubrics_metrics.description: 'nothing more contributes than frequent writing; most of the Orations we are now possessed of were written not before they were spoken, but some time afterwards.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligent preparation, composition, and revision are essential. Some orators prepared intensely (dictating to amanuenses, spending days in study) and cultivated their craft by writing and private declamation; indolence or refusal to write is an avoidable failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter expertise and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers praised for being 'well acquainted with the Grecian literature' or 'the best lawyer of his time' — legal and literary knowledge enhanced eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mastery of relevant knowledge (law, history, literature) strengthens arguments, examples, and authority (ethos). Learned speakers could draw richer references and craft more persuasive narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animated delivery and physical presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of a speaker leaving his study 'with so much life in his eyes, and such an ardent glow upon his countenance' and delivering with 'uncommon force and dignity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical animation, expression, and presence during delivery amplify persuasion. Preparation should include rehearsing delivery; audience perception of energy and conviction can determine a speech's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic emotional and ethical tactics (soothe, alarm, implore compassion, enlarge on moral topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Servius Galba 'digressing from his subject to embellish and diversify it, --soothing or alarming the passions, exhibiting every circumstance in the strongest light, imploring the compassion of his audience, and artfully enlarging on those topics, or general principles of Prudence or Morality...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical maneuvers strategically: digressions, vivid presentation of circumstances, appeals to pity or fear, and moral framing can be effective. The text treats these as deliberate techniques of a consummate orator; they should be employed to support the argument's main thrust rather than for mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate models but preserve substance and vigor
rubrics_metrics.description: On borrowing 'the Attic neatness' — 'provided they borrow the blood and the healthy juices, as well as the bones and membranes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation of admired styles (e.g., Attic neatness) is valuable but must preserve intellectual vigor and authenticity; don't copy surface features at the expense of strength and substance. Model after masters but integrate vitality, not mere form.
